step_by_step_reasoning: The architecture diagram shows GE Avio's expense management system built on AWS. The flow starts with an employee authenticating via a corporate OpenID provider, which routes through ELB to ECS and an Authorization Lambda function to complete authorization. Once authorized, the user downloads a Single Page Application from Docker running on ECS, which communicates with an API Gateway container on ECS. The API Gateway forwards requests to around 20 core business logic Lambda functions. These Lambdas manage ticket metadata stored in DynamoDB, while financial document attachments are uploaded and stored in S3, encrypted at rest using AWS KMS.

graph.name: GE Avio Expense Management Architecture
graph.notes: Serverless application for GE Avio managing special expenses for employees, replacing a legacy system to handle quarterly traffic spikes.

nodes.notes: GE Avio employees managing quarterly special expense tickets.

nodes.name: OPEN ID

nodes.name: ECS

nodes.name: Lambda (Authorization)
nodes.notes: Lambda function dedicated to user authorization validation against OpenID.

nodes.name: Lambda (Business Logic)
nodes.notes: Approximately 20 Lambda functions implementing core application features (ticket creation, editing, state shifts).

nodes.notes: NoSQL database used to store ticket metadata.

nodes.name: S3
nodes.notes: S3 bucket storing financial document attachments, encrypted at rest with KMS.

edges.notes: User authenticates against corporate OpenID provider.
OpenID forwards auth requests through ELB.
ELB forwards request to ECS container.
Authorization Lambda validates identity with OpenID system.
User downloads Single Page Application (SPA) hosted on Docker in ECS.
User SPA collaborates directly with API Gateway container running on ECS.
API Gateway routes requests to business logic Lambdas.
Business logic Lambdas persist ticket metadata in DynamoDB.
Application uploads financial attachments to S3 (KMS encrypted).
